question.brief: Marek, 35, has 100,000 PLN invested: 60% in a broad share fund and 40% in a bond fund. He adds 1,000 PLN every month. Write his rule for the next 36 months. Two tests must pass: in a long rally his mix stays between 50% and 70% shares, and in a crash he never drops below 40% shares, so no panic selling. Rebalancing costs 0.1% of the money moved. Then we test your rule in other markets.

reveal.editorial: The reference rule rebalances only when the mix is more than 5 points away from 60/40, and invests new money in the target mix. In a rally it sells some shares at high prices; in a crash it buys shares at low prices, which is the opposite of panic selling. Rebalancing every month keeps the mix tightest but pays the most fees. Waiting for 10 points lets the mix leave the 50-70% band before acting. A rule decided in calm times is what keeps you from selling at the bottom.

question.brief: Ania, 27, earns 6,500 PLN a month after tax and needs 4,800 PLN for essentials. She has 8,000 PLN saved and no debt. Write her monthly rule for the next 24 months: how much goes to her safety buffer and how much is invested. Money she does not assign is spent. Two tests must pass: she never uses her credit card during a 2-month job loss, and she invests at least 15,000 PLN over the two years. Then we test your rule against other surprises.

reveal.editorial: The reference rule does three things in order. If there is card debt, it pays it off first, because 20% a year beats any expected return. Until the buffer covers 3 months of essential costs, it saves. After that, it invests. A 2-month buffer passes the required tests but fails more of the surprises; a 6-month buffer survives almost everything but invests less. There is no single right size: it depends on how secure the income is.
